title: Randomized: Fisher-Yates Shuffle
oneLiner: Shuffle an array so every order is equally likely: walk from the end, swapping each position with a random position at or before it. The random picks are given, so the result can be checked.
keyTakeaway: For i from n - 1 down to 1, pick j uniformly from 0 to i and swap a[i] with a[j]. Position i is then final, filled by a uniform choice among the values still unplaced, which makes all n! orders equally likely in O(n). Picking j from the WHOLE array each time looks similar but is biased.
explanation:
Shuffle nums using the Fisher-Yates algorithm. Randomness can't be graded, so the random numbers are given to you: picks[t] is the random index the generator returned at step t. Step 0 handles i = n - 1, step 1 handles i = n - 2, and so on down to i = 1, and picks[t] is always between 0 and i. Return the array after all the swaps. For nums [1, 2, 3, 4] with picks [0, 0, 0]: swap positions 3 and 0, then 2 and 0, then 1 and 0, giving [2, 3, 4, 1].

The algorithm: for i from n - 1 down to 1, let j = picks[n - 1 - i] (in real code, rng.Next(i + 1)), and swap a[i] with a[j]. Think of the array as two parts: the unplaced prefix a[0..i] and the finished suffix after it. Each step picks one of the i + 1 unplaced values uniformly and moves it into position i, where it stays.

Why it is fair: the last position gets each value with probability 1/n, the next one gets each remaining value with probability 1/(n - 1), and so on. Multiplying, every one of the n! permutations has probability 1/n!. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

The famous bug is swapping a[i] with a[rng.Next(n)], choosing from the whole array every time. That makes n^n equally likely sequences of choices, and n^n is not divisible by n! for n > 2, so some orders must come up more often than others. Sorting by random keys (OrderBy(x => rng.Next())) is unbiased only if keys never tie, and it costs O(n log n). In real code, C# has Random.Shuffle (.NET 8 and later) and Python has random.shuffle, both Fisher-Yates.

The visualization shuffles [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] with picks [2, 3, 0, 1]; highlighted cells are final.

i = 2: the pick is j = 0, one of 3 unplaced slots. Swap positions 2 and 0; position 2 now holds 10 for good.
i = 1: the pick is j = 1, one of 2 unplaced slots. Swap positions 1 and 1; position 1 now holds 20 for good.

recognitionSignals: Shuffle, deal cards, random permutation, or "each order equally likely".
Random sampling without replacement from an array (stop Fisher-Yates after k steps).
gotchas: Choosing j from 0 to n - 1 every step instead of 0 to i biases the result.
rng.Next(i) excludes i itself; use rng.Next(i + 1) so an element can stay where it is.
Map step t to i = n - 1 - t: the first pick belongs to the last position.
confusableWith: Reservoir Sampling also gives every item an equal chance, but over a stream whose length you don't know in advance.
Randomized quicksort uses randomness to choose pivots for speed; the output is deterministic. Here the randomness is the output.

complexity.note: One swap per position from the back. The shuffle itself is in place; this version copies the input first (O(n) if you count it).
